newsitem.title: UK: British ministers discuss tobacco ad ban.
newsitem.headline: British ministers discuss tobacco ad ban.

text.p: British government ministers and health officials held a "smoking summit" on Monday and said they would discuss banning tobacco advertising and sponsorship of sport.
Tobacco industry representatives objected to being left out of the conference, saying they could help, but the government said it did not need their input.

"Our decision to organise the summit demonstrates our commitment to take the action that is necessary to reduce the number of people whose health is ruined and whose lives are shortened by smoking," Britain's Health Secretary Frank Dobson told the summit as it opened.
"And let me make it clear -- the new government is determined to take action. This summit is not a side show by the health department," he added.
"The tobacco industry kills 120,000 of its British customers every year. So it has to recruit new smokers to make up for the thousands it kills."
Tessa Jowell, minister for public health, said experts from Europe, the United States and Australia would offer advice at the one-day meeting.
"We will certainly take what lessons we can from other countries and apply them here," she told BBC radio.
"We are fortified by the evidence that a ban on advertising has an effect on the rate at which young people smoke."
The new Labour government said shortly after its election in May that it would severely restrict tobacco advertising and sponsorship.
"Young people are particularly sensitive to the glamorous images of tobacco associated with sport," Jowell said.

A spokesman for British-American Tobacco said his industry could offer valuable research on advertising bans. "There is substantial evidence from around the world that advertising bans limit competition, not smoking," Brendan Brady told BBC radio.

"The government is the largest single stakeholder in the tobacco industry, receiving around 80 pence ($1.30) from every one pound ($1.65) smokers spend on tobacco, yet the government has chosen to exclude tobacco companies from discussions about future tobacco policy."
But ministers, who said they may also discuss possible lawsuits against the industry, made their attitudes towards tobacco companies clear.
"If tobacco were introduced today it would not stand the remotest chance of being a legal product. There is no safe level of smoking," Jowell said.
She said the government would consider a package of measures that could include bans on advertising, sponsorship and possibly on smoking in public places, public education and higher taxes.
The government said on Monday that 61 percent of the British public backed a ban on tobacco advertising. Jowell noted new government figures showed teenagers were taking up smoking at younger ages.
"I dread the thought of today's trendy youngsters filling tomorrow's cancer wards," Jowell told the summit.

"New figures today show that at the age of 15, 28 percent of boys and 33 percent of girls are regular smokers. No responsible government can look at these figures without wanting to do all in its power to reverse the trend."
